title: Pointer Basics
html:
A pointer is a variable that holds the address of another object. & takes an address, * follows one. Pointers are what make C fast, flexible — and dangerous.

Pointer — an object whose value is a memory address, together with the type of what lives there. int *p means “p points to an int” — the type tells the compiler how many bytes to read through it and how far p + 1 moves.

Printing addresses

Key point

%p expects a void *; cast other pointer types. Addresses differ between runs because of address space layout randomisation.

NULL and pointer states

Valid

Points to a live object of the right type — the only state you may dereference.

NULL

p = NULL; — explicitly points nowhere. Test with if (p) / if (p != NULL). Dereferencing it crashes.

Wild / uninitialised

int *p; holds garbage. Dereferencing it writes to a random address.

Dangling

Pointed to an object whose lifetime ended (freed or out of scope).

Dereferencing NULL

Watch out

int* a, b; declares one pointer (a) and one int (b) — the * binds to the name, not the type. Write int *a, *b; or one declaration per line.

What is the size of a pointer?

It depends on the platform, not on the pointed-to type: 8 bytes on 64-bit systems, 4 on 32-bit. sizeof(char *) == sizeof(double *) on all mainstream platforms (function pointers can differ on exotic ones).

What is the difference between NULL, 0 and '\0'?

NULL is a null pointer constant (usually ((void *)0)). 0 is an integer that also acts as a null pointer constant in pointer context. '\0' is the NUL character (an int with value 0) used to terminate strings. They compare equal to zero but mean different things — use each in its own role. C23 adds nullptr.

Why use pointers at all?

To let functions modify caller data (out-parameters), to pass large objects cheaply, to work with dynamically allocated memory, to build linked data structures (lists, trees, graphs), to iterate arrays efficiently and to implement callbacks via function pointers.
